title: Second brick plant no quick fix for WA housing shortage
text:
Stated Claim / Post Context:
Second brick plant no quick fix for WA housing shortage

Taxpayers are funding the reopening of the Austral factory, which the government hopes will help address the shortage of bricks plaguing the construction industry.

Actual Article Body:
Emergency

中文新闻

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

TOK PISIN

Topic:Housing Construction Industry

Austral Bricks shut its WA facility in 2023 due to a lack of demand. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Western Australia's state government will pay up to $4 million to Austral Bricks to reopen its plant in the state.

The Sydney-based company shut down its WA factory mid-2023, and the only other manufacturer, Midland Brick, has struggled to keep up with demand.

WA Deputy Premier Rita Saffioti said the funding was an example of the government jumping in to address the needs of critical industries.

Western Australian taxpayers will fork out up to $4 million to restart a second brick making facility in the state as the construction industry continues to grapple with labour and raw material shortages.

The state was left with just one brickmaker when Austral closed its Cardup brickworks in mid-2023.

Since then, the government says the number of detached homes starting construction has grown by more than 50 per cent, leaving the remaining manufacturer — Midland Brick — struggling to keep up with demand.

A surge in demand for housing over the last three years, driven by an influx of people into WA, has contributed to the brick shortage.  (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

In an effort to address the shortfall, the state government will now give $3 million to Austral to re-open its facility, which is expected to increase production by up to 15 per cent.

"This is making sure we do everything possible to continue the momentum of building more homes and also reducing the challenges of increased costs [of] bricks," Treasurer Rita Saffioti said.

Deputy Premier Saffioti said the government was helping the industry "get on with it" by providing funding. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Asked why state money was required to kickstart the project given the high demand, Ms Saffioti said the government was supporting industries in critical sectors "to get on with it".

Industry executives who attended the funding announcement, made at a construction site in the Perth suburb of Sinagra, were unanimous in their support.

"Still not enough, so we've still got an issue, but it's certainly a large help," ABN Group managing director Dale Alcock said.

Industry veteran Alcock says the Austral plant will go some way towards addressing shortages, but costs remain high. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

The industry veteran said the company, one of the state's largest homebuilders, had around 100 sites waiting on bricks. He urged the government to look into other ways to increase supply.

Mr Alcock said an "allocation system" used by Midland Brick showed there was "not enough [bricks] currently to go around".

“At the moment, the industry is more concerned about availability than cost,” Mr Alcock said.

Master Builders WA CEO, Matt Moran, said having a large enough workforce was also critical to the industry's future.

Mr Moran wants labour shortages to also be addressed. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"We need to double down and invest in trades. We need to promote trades more, attract people to apprenticeships," he said.

The government is offering Austral an extra $500,000 if it can resume operations by March.

The company will also get another $500,000 incentive if it produces at least 17 million bricks in its first year.

However, Housing Industry Association WA CEO, Michael McGowan, warned home owners that this would not provide a quick fix to the delays plaguing the industry, and urged people to be patient over the next 12 months

Michael McGowan urged homeowners to be patient with the industry, which is still facing delays. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"There is going to be a little bit more time before these bricks become available, and the brick layers and the builders are working really hard to deliver the homes that are currently in the pipeline," he said.
